thread.title: The Dark Side of the Boom

author: Randall W. Forsyth
title: The Dark Side of the Boom

organizations.name: centers for disease control and prevention

text:
Photo: iStockphoto By Randall W. Forsyth June 8, 2018 1:04 p.m. ET To call these the best of times and the worst of times may be a cliché, but is apt nonetheless.
Led by the surging stocks of the big technology companies whose products occupy so much of our modern lives, the Nasdaq Composite index last week hit a record, capping a gain of 23% over the past year. U.S. households’ wealth also topped $100 trillion in the first quarter for the first time, which means they nearly doubled their net worth from the low in 2009 after the financial crisis. And with unemployment at just 3.8%, there are more job openings than jobless available to fill them.
Last week also brought depressing news of suicides, not just of wealthy, successful figures such as Kate Spade and Anthony Bourdain, but of regular folks not admired by millions who struggle with deprivation, both material and otherwise. There were nearly 45,000 suicides in the U.S. in 2016, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported, more than twice the number of homicides. That followed previous news that the birth rate fell to a 30-year low last year, another rejection of life that typically coincides with hard times, not good ones.
With apologies to those who come here for insights about what to buy or sell on Monday morning, these are things to contemplate on Saturday or Sunday. By Monday, investors will be watching a dizzying parade of events that might leave little time for contemplation of such matters.
The Group of Seven will have wound up what will certainly be a contentious confab in which President Donald Trump is expected to be piled on by the heads of the other six big industrialized economies over U.S. tariffs. Then he’s expected to make an early exit for the Singapore summit on Tuesday with North Korea. Will there be “denuclearization,” however defined? Markets aren’t holding their breath for a breakthrough.
Tuesday brings an eagerly awaited decision in the U.S. case to block the megamerger of AT&T (ticker: T) with Time Warner (TWX), which could have major implications for other big deals. Then, investors can turn their attention to the key events of the week—policy meetings of the central banks overseeing the world’s major market economies.
That would be the Federal Reserve, whose Open Market Committee winds up a two-day meeting on Wednesday, after which it will all but certainly announce a 25-basis-point (one-quarter of a percentage point) increase in its federal-funds target, from the current range of 1.5% to 1.75%. (For achingly technical reasons, the actual rise will be 20 basis points.)
Of vastly more interest will be the FOMC’s projections for the rest of 2018, into 2019, and beyond. According to a Bloomberg analysis of fed-funds futures, there’s a 73% probability of an additional hike of 25 basis points or more at the panel’s Sept. 25-26 meeting. But after that, the outlook gets cloudier. The so-called dot plot of the FOMC members’ projections shows significantly higher fed-funds rates than the market is discounting for 2019 and 2020, a reflection of the central bankers’ continual overestimation of where they think rates will go. All of which proves Yogi Berra’s insight about the difficulty of making forecasts, especially about the future.
While the Fed tweaks its economic and rate outlook, there may be an equal focus on the European Central Bank’s Thursday meeting. ECB officials seem likely to consider the beginning of the end of its massive bond purchases, now 30 billion euros ($35.3 billion) a month. While the Fed has been shrinking its balance sheet, the ECB’s quantitative easing has been a key source of global liquidity. The Bank of Japan also meets on Friday, but is expected to maintain its expansionary policy, given that inflation is still short of its 2% target.
Market liquidity, especially the dollar variety, last week became a key concern. Emerging market central bankers, notably India’s head (discussed below), warned the Fed of the global consequences of its policy normalization. A stronger dollar and higher U.S. interest rates are a double whammy for emerging market borrowers in greenbacks.
Then there was the mysterious, but transitory, flash crash in Treasury yields (and spike in prices) on Thursday afternoon. As relayed by John Brady, managing director for global institutional sales at Chicago futures broker R.J. O’Brien, the episode suggests that the Fed is possibly losing control of interest-rate prospects to the Treasury.
As stronger growth collides with greater Treasury borrowing, liquidity is absorbed. At the same time, central banks are moving away from accommodation—not a plus for asset prices.
Separate but Unequal Corporate America is flush with cash, but like wealth throughout the economy, it’s highly concentrated in relatively few hands.
According to RDQ Economics’ parsing of the latest Financial Accounts of the U.S. (formerly called the Flow of Funds) release from the Federal Reserve , liquid assets of nonfinancial corporations rose $66.7 billion in the first quarter, to $2.7 trillion. On the other side of their collective balance sheets, their aggregate debt-to-equity ratios edged up to a “still historically low 34.2% from 33.4% in the fourth quarter”—and less than half at the peak of the past decade’s credit boom.
Viewed another way, corporate cash was up 14.5% from a year ago in the first quarter, according to Evercore ISI. “And as a share of GDP, it’s a moon shot,” the firm adds, surging to 13.54% of nominal output. While that’s good news, the bad news is that corporate debt has surged—less than cash, to be sure, but still by 50% over the past decade.
And why not? Given that the main countercyclical policy utilized after the financial crisis was for central banks to lower interest rates to zero (and below, in Europe and Japan) while buying boatloads of bonds with printed money—a process politely called “quantitative easing”—borrowing was the route to riches.
Of course, much of that debt went for share repurchases, which has been a mighty benefit to the stock market, as our recent cover story discusses ( “Why the Buyback Boom Is Bullish for Investors,” May 12). S&P 500 companies are projected to announce buybacks totaling $650 billion—including Apple ’s (ticker: AAPL) blockbuster $100 billion program —exceeding the $589 billion record set in 2007.
According to Bank of America Merrill Lynch credit analysts, buybacks hit a record for the investment-grade nonfinancial companies in the first quarter at $123 billion, up from $82 billion in the previous quarter and $66 billion in the third quarter of 2017. Two-thirds came from 24 investment-grade issuers with large foreign cash holdings.
But as MacroMavens’ Stephanie Pomboy also points out, that liquidity is spread quite unevenly among the S&P 500. The top 25 companies in the benchmark index account for 56% of the $1.9 trillion in cash held by the index components, according to statistics from Moody’s Investors Service. And the top 50 hold 68% of the cash, while the bottom 250 of the S&P 500 essentially hold zero.
While the repatriation of U.S. corporations’ profits held overseas has helped pay for buybacks, it also has drained those dollars held in banks abroad, causing dislocations in the global banking system. In essence, this shift has hampered the ability of foreign banks to expand their balance sheets, writes Steve Blitz, chief U.S. economist at TS Lombard.
He estimates U.S. corporations’ earnings held abroad fell at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $632 billion in the first quarter, which he compared to the $160 billion SAAR of decline in the Fed’s securities holdings. Blitz opines this effect has had an even bigger impact on emerging markets than the reduction of the Fed’s balance sheet, which is being blamed by some monetary authorities abroad for the weakness of EM currencies.
Newsletter Sign-up One of them, Urjit Patel, governor of the Reserve Bank of India, last week wrote in a Financial Times op-ed article that U.S. policies have a double whammy on dollar liquidity for global markets. The Fed will increase the pace of reduction of its holdings of Treasury and agency mortgage-backed securities to $50 billion a month by October. By December 2019, the U.S. central bank will have pared its holdings by $1 trillion.
As of Wednesday, the Fed’s assets totaled $4.279 trillion, a reduction of $143.68 billion from a year ago. In other words, the wind-down of its balance sheet is still in the early stages.
While the Fed is reducing its holdings of Treasuries, the U.S. government is ramping up its sale of debt securities to cover the increased budget deficit resulting from this year’s tax cuts, Patel continues. Net issuance by the federal government is projected to total $1.169 trillion in the current year and $1.171 trillion in 2019. In the first quarter, federal government debt surged at a 15.3% annual rate, according to Fed data.
Patel urged the Fed to reduce the pace of balance-sheet reduction to accommodate the increased debt issuance resulting from the tax cuts to ameliorate “the shortage of dollar liquidity caused by higher U.S. government borrowing.” The Fed, however, will take international factors into account to the extent they affect the domestic economy, not those abroad.
The bottom line is that macroeconomic policies have provided a surfeit of cash for the top tier of U.S. corporations to distribute to their shareholders . At the same time, the rest of the world is far from flush and could face a tightening of dollar liquidity.
In the June 10 Up and Down Wall Street column, the most recent unemployment rate was incorrectly stated. It was 3.8% in May, not 3.9%.
